new_statements.quote: Dentro de los idiomas Mayas hay tres sistemas diferentes de acentuación (Kaufman, este volumen) y dentro del Mam se encuentran los tres. En Tacaná, el acento cae en la última silaba, con la excepción de algunos enclíticos que nunca llevan acento (Munson 1984). [...] En Ostuncalco el acento cae en la penúltima silaba, y otra vez hay enclíticos que no tienen ningún efecto sobre la acentuación. Ejemplos: t-xmílaal 'su cuerpo', kaab'áje 'anteayer', kyaáje' 'cuatro'; pero no hay efecto de enclitico: nxaájab'-e' 'mis caites'. En Ixtahuacán el acento cae en una sílaba "pesada".
new_statements.translation: Within the Mayan languages there are three different stress systems (Kaufman, this volume) and all three are found within Mam. In Tacaná, stress falls on the last syllable, except for some enclitics that never bear stress (Munson 1984). [...] In Ostuncalco stress falls on the penultimate syllable, and again there are enclitics that have no effect on stress placement. Examples: t-xmílaal 'his body', kaab'áje 'day before yesterday', kyaáje' 'four'; but no effect of an enclitic: nxaájab'-e' 'my sandals'. In Ixtahuacán stress falls on a 'heavy' syllable.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (569 pp., archive.org item LecturaSobreLaLinguisticaMaya1, ClearScan text layer read with extracted text). England, 'El Mam: semejanzas y diferencias regionales', chapter starts printed p. 221 = PDF p. 245; sec. 1.2.3 'Acento' is on printed p. 225 = PDF p. 249 exactly as the locator says. The text layer reads: 'Dentro de los idiomas Mayas hay tres sistemas diferentes de acentuación (Kaufman, este volumen) y dentro del Mam se encuentran los tres. En Tacaná, el acento cae en la última silaba, con la excepción de algunos enclíticos que nunca llevan acento ( Mu nson 1 984). Ejemplos: ub'éch flor / wiinqí'n veinte / yaají después / tx'eemb'eén la cortada; pero no en enclítico: twaak…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Southern Mam (San Juan Ostuncalco, Quetzaltenango, England's representative town for the southern region) word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the word, irrespective of vowel length or glottal stop (her comparative table p. 226 shows Ostuncalco aátz'an, suúb'an, q'ób'xeek, wíinqi'n, eéwi, t-xmílaal, all penult, including q'ób'xeek with an unstressed final long vowel); enclitics are outside the stress domain and do not shift stress (nxaájab'-e'). This contrasts with Northern Mam (Ixtahuacán: weight-driven) and Western Mam (Tacaná: final).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress for Ostuncalco.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics never count for stress (stress stays on the host's penult). Related length facts (pp. 225-227): Ostuncalco historically shortened post-tonic long vowels, so long vowels after the stressed vowel are generally short, though more than one long vowel per word is still possible; final long vowels shorten in open or n-final syllables even when stressed (njaa-ye' 'mi casa' vs tja 'su casa'). Monosyllables are identical across regions. Kaufman 1990:67 (same volume) adds that Mayan stress is fully predictable in native vocabulary and clitics are unstressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation forms (host word excluding enclitics); statement is for the San Juan Ostuncalco variety, explicitly chosen (p. 222) to represent 'el Mam del sur' (rest of San Marcos and the Mam part of Quetzaltenango); Kaufman 1990:67 generalizes 'Mam del Sur' = penultimate (his Type C). Modern second-hand confirmations: England 2017:501 as reported by Elkins 2023:70, 209 and Elkins & Kuo 2023:1 ('Southern Mam.. regularly penultimate regardless of syllable weight', Cajolá cited via Pérez & Jiménez 1997).
new_statements.identity_note: mams1234 is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry for retired ISO 639-3 [mms] 'Mam, Southern' (merged into [mam] in 2009); the language-level languoid is Mam mamm1241, which the catalog already holds with the Northern (Ixtahuacán) weight-sensitive rule (England 1975/1983). The statement quoted here is specifically for the San Juan Ostuncalco variety (Quetzaltenango), which England 1990:222 selects to represent 'el Mam del sur' (rest of San Marcos + Mam-speaking Quetzaltenango = old Ethnologue 'Southern Mam'); Kaufman 1990:67 generalizes it to 'Mam del Sur', and Elkins 2023 (citing England 2017:501, Pérez & Jiménez 1997) reports the same penultimate rule for Cajolá, another Southern town. So the Southern entry differs typologically from the mamm1241 catalog entry (fixed penult vs weight-sensitive) and from Western/Tacaná Mam (fixed final).

En Tacaná, el acento cae en la última silaba, con la excepción de algunos enclíticos que nunca llevan acento (Munson 1984). [...] En Ostuncalco el acento cae en la penúltima silaba, y otra vez hay enclíticos que no tienen ningún efecto sobre la acentuación. sources.note: Sec. 1.2.3 Acento, pp. 225-226: three-town comparison. Ostuncalco (south): stress on the penultimate syllable, enclitics have no effect on stress (exx. t-xmílaal, kaab'áje, kyaáje', nxaájab'-e'); Tacaná (west): final syllable; Ixtahuacán (north): heavy syllable (long V > V before last glottal stop > last root V before C). Adds that Ostuncalco shortened post-tonic long vowels historically, may still have more than one long vowel per word, and shortens final long vowels in open or n-final syllables even when stressed.
